5e510b1491894992: KUALA LUMPUR, September 29 — The 25th edition of Anugerah Industri Muzik (AIM) proved to be a momentous one for singer-songwriter Mimifly following her five-award haul.

Her single Temberang won Best Music Video and Best Electronic/Pop Dance, while Serumpun earned her Best Festive Song and Song with the Most User-Generated Video on TikTok. Nara, meanwhile, won Best Musical Arrangement in a Song.

Speaking to local media following her landslide win, Mimifly (real name Shamimi Amalina Norhisham) said she was thankful for the recognition, but her conviction to create art remained unchanged by achievements or failures.
“I don’t want to stop creating just because of achievements or failures. I want to keep creating just for the sake of it.
“So it doesn’t really matter if I win or lose because I still have a lot of pieces (of work) to assemble,” she said.
The hiatus
Before going solo, Mimifly was part of local hip hop group One Nation Emcees, where she was the sole female member and was heavily involved in composing and writing for the group.
The now 39-year-old began transitioning into a solo artist around 2016 through singles such as Goyang Fly and Super Fly, and officially left the group in 2020, the same year she went on hiatus.
“I made my comeback in late 2024 after a four-year hiatus during which I put out no music — and I was honestly miserable during that time.
“I felt completely lost when I wasn’t working. Coming back with Angkat, which won at AIM 24, and now following it up with Temberang, I’m deeply grateful for how everything has unfolded.
“As an anak seni (artist), this is the path I’ve chosen, and I’m determined to keep going,” she said.

Reflecting on her lowest point, Mimi said she not only struggled to find her footing as an independent artist, but also experienced countless failures and faced snarky comments from people in the industry.

“For many years, whenever I worked on something, people just wouldn’t believe in me. They said I was too old to still be in the industry, they said my prime time was over, and even when I gave them one song after another, they just wouldn’t believe in my work.

“Old and irrelevant — I would almost always hear people say that about me, and I ended up doing everything on my own. God has given me the chance to eventually succeed and to show everyone the power of not giving up,” she said.
Apart from maintaining her self-belief, Mimi also credited her success to a solid support system, including her mother, other family members and her small team.
The comeback
Mimi was at the point of almost quitting music until she met producer Bo Amir Iqram, who inspired her to continue her journey.
“When I first met Bo Amir Iqram and heard his sound, I got goosebumps. I instantly felt that he was the right musical partner for me.
“At the time, I didn’t even have a management team — it was just the two of us making music together throughout 2024. We were in and out of the studio the entire year.

“Initially, I had no plans to release anything just yet, but once we recorded Angkat, everything clicked, and I knew it was time to put it out into the world,” she said, adding that Bo was among the first to believe in her, followed by her current manager, Shah.
Now back in the industry and enjoying renewed success, Mimi emphasised that her goal is not to be the best artist in the country, but rather to be completely irreplaceable — the “one and only”.
“It’s not about proving who among us artists is the best. I just want to be the only one doing what I do.
“I hope this opens the eyes of younger artists — if you truly believe in your artistic vision, you shouldn’t worry about what anyone else says,” she said.
3f4bd2c688799311: KARIYACHALLI, Sept 29 — Under a blazing sun, workers crouch on a shrinking island off India’s southern coast, threading bright green seagrass shoots onto wooden frames before anchoring them onto the ocean floor.

Restoration work on Kariyachalli island hopes to rebuild its natural defences with artificial reefs, transplanted corals and seagrass meadows, in a bid to slow erosion and protect the mainland from surging seas.

“If you are not able to provide that resilience, you are absolutely at the mercy of vulnerabilities of storm surges, cyclonic storms or sea-level rise and also erosion,” senior state official Supriya Sahu told AFP.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows an underwater view of a coral restoration site near Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India’s Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
AFP travelled by boat to the protected island after being granted exclusive access by the foreign ministry.

Kariyachalli, which is part of a chain of 21 islands in southern Tamil Nadu state, has lost more than 80 per cent of its landmass over the past half century and could disappear entirely by 2036 if erosion is left unchecked.
Government estimates show Kariyachalli shrank from 20.85 hectares in 1969 to just 3.14 hectares last year.
The coral reefs in the Gulf of Mannar, where Kariyachalli and other islands are located, also play a vital role in softening the impact of natural disasters, such as the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
More than 8,000 people were killed in Tamil Nadu during the tsunami, but marine scientists say these ecosystems acted as a crucial natural barrier and prevented a much larger disaster from happening.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows members of the fishing community tying seagrass shoots onto jute twines for restoration work to protect Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India's Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
Falling reef cover
“This was because these tiny islands, seagrass and coral beds absorb the impact,” said K. Diraviya Raj, an associate professor at the Suganthi Devadason Marine Research Institute.
The Gulf of Mannar is among Asia’s richest marine environments, home to coral reefs, endangered dugongs and hundreds of fish species.
But decades of human activity and climate change have steadily weakened the ecosystem.
Coral mining in the 1960s and 1970s severely damaged reefs around the islands. Pollution, over-fishing and coral bleaching caused by warming seas have also added pressure.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows fishing community members getting into the boat to travel to Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India’s Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
Around Kariyachalli, reef cover fell from roughly 500 hectares in 2005 to 197 hectares in 2021.
The restoration, part of a US$4.79 million (RM19.55 million) state conservation programme, includes the deployment of about 8,500 artificial reef modules around the island.
The bulky structures, each weighing several tonnes, are being lowered into carefully selected locations around Kariyachalli.
Designed using data on seabed conditions, currents and wave patterns, they are intended to break the force of incoming waves while creating new surfaces for corals to colonise.
Experts are also transplanting corals and restoring seagrass meadows that help stabilise sediments and provide nursery grounds for marine life.
The deployment phase is expected to finish by the end of September, after which the site will be monitored for at least four years.
For local residents, the project offers a chance to earn some extra money.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows fishing community members tying seagrass shoots onto a casuarina frame for restoration work protecting Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India's Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
Marine heatwaves
Among them is saltpan worker Devkani, 47, who travels 25 minutes by boat from the mainland to prepare seagrass frames.
“We had to borrow loans earlier at high interest rates to make ends meet during lean months at saltpans,” she told AFP.
“But this year because of this sea-based work, we didn’t have to.”
Though there have been some strides, scientists acknowledge that warming oceans have created significant challenges to reef restoration.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows a scientific diver holding a transplanted coral from the restoration site underwater near Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India’s Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
A severe bleaching incident hit the region in 2024, killing large numbers of corals and raising questions about whether restoration efforts can keep pace with climate change.
Researcher Raj argued that the worsening outlook makes intervention even more necessary.
“What we are doing is restoring corals to keep the biomass intact,” he said.
“So, in a way corals will adapt themselves for this deteriorating scenario of changing climatic conditions and will survive to form the future reef.”
Scientists are also searching for naturally heat-resistant coral species that might better withstand future marine heatwaves.
There are already signs of encouragement elsewhere in the Gulf of Mannar.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows fishing community members tying seagrass shoots onto a casuarina frame for restoration work protecting Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India's Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
On nearby Vaan Island, restoration involving about 10,000 artificial reef modules helped recover part of the lost landmass.
On Shingle Island, transplanted corals endured a 2024 bleaching event better than older colonies.
“Vaan island restoration results were very promising,” said wildlife warden Akhil Thampi. “That’s why we went towards Kariyachalli island restoration.”
But for seagrass worker Martina, the reason to support the project is personal.
“Growing seagrass increases the reproduction of fish and saves the ecosystem,” said Martina, 29, who goes by one name.
“This is useful to us and improves our livelihood.” — AFP
580e7ab28145f41a: MANCHESTER, Sept 29 — Manchester City’s fate in a legal battle with the Premier League is yet to be sealed, but reports they have been found guilty on widespread financial misconduct has sparked speculation of what comes next.
The dominant Premier League force for more than a decade, swingeing sanctions against City would send shockwaves through English football.

Rival clubs are set to launch their own legal action seeking hundreds of millions of pounds in compensation, while there is debate over whether some of City’s many titles and trophies over the past 15 years could be stripped.
AFP Sports looks at the next steps and potential fall out from the case:
Sanction and appeals process
The Athletic first reported on Friday that City had been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges they faced.
However, no sanction has yet been approved.
Even once a decision is made on how City will be punished, should they be found guilty, the club are almost certain to appeal.
In a letter to City fans on Saturday, the club’s chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said: “Our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.”
A case that began after German outlet Der Spiegel published leaked documents from City executives in 2018, could still take a lengthy time to fully resolve.
According to Premier League rules, the sanction can vary from a points deduction, a fine or even expulsion from the division.

Everton and Nottingham Forest were handed points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of financial sustainability rules. On that basis, City would face almost certain relegation if found guilty of over 100 charges.
Whether the sanction is applied before an appeal is heard will be another bone of contention.
If it is, City could face relegation before overturning any guilty verdict.
On the other hand, if City, who currently sit top of the table, are not punished until after an appeal, it could cost other clubs their place in the top-flight or lucrative European qualification.

Even after the Premier League process if over, there is also the chance that City’s Abu-Dhabi backed owners seek redress in England’s High Court if they challenge a legal issue regarding how the arbitration process was conducted.
Who stands to gain?
City’s rivals were quick to revel in the news of their potential demise.
“Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet,” posted former Manchester United defender Rio Ferdinand, who was part of the United team to finish second to City in the 2011/12 season.
The reality is that stripping and retroactively awarding titles is a messy process.
City’s charges relate to the period between 2009 and 2018. In that time they won four league titles, with United and Liverpool twice finishing second in those seasons.
Yet City have won another four since, arguably built on foundations that were fraudulently gained.
They also won four League Cups and one FA Cup, the club’s first trophy for 35 years, in the period between 2009 and 2018.
“I don’t seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either,” Tony Pulis, whose Stoke side lost the 2011 FA Cup final to City, told the BBC.
“A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely. But I still feel cheated.”
A more likely source of recompense for clubs that missed out is through financial compensation.
In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35 million (US$46 million) after they edged out the Clarets to Premier League survival in the same season they broke financial sustainability rules.
What about City’s stars?
Less than a month ago, City completed the biggest ever transfer spend in one window, splashing out around £460 million on the likes of Enzo Fernandez, Elliott Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi.
The impending verdict on the charges has to this point made little impact on City’s ability to attract and retain their star names.
Talismanic striker Erling Haaland signed a nine-year contract in 2025 that could keep him tied down till his 34th birthday.
How many, if any, of the players managed to negotiate exit clauses in the case City were heavily sanctioned remains to be seen. — AFP

a8fd9bb11cf5c7c2: KUALA LUMPUR: VS Industry Bhd reported a smaller net loss of RM22 million in the fourth quarter ended July 31, 2026 (Q4 FY26), than RM33 million a year earlier, as revenue increased 16.3 per cent year-on-year to RM998.6 million.

The increase in revenue during the quarter was supported by higher sales orders from key customers despite higher impairment loss on plant and equipment amounting to RM39.7 million, said VS in a filing with Bursa Malaysia.

However, the electronic manufacturing services group recorded a net loss of RM53.82 million for FY26, compared with a net profit of RM36.71 million a year earlier, as VS is affected by lower orders from key customers affected by soft consumer sentiments globally, it said.
VS Industry said the weaker order intake affected overall production capacity utilisation, while customers also implemented cost optimisation measures.
Revenue for the year slipped 3.6 per cent to RM3.65 billion from RM3.78 billion.
VS Industry did not declare a dividend for the quarter, bringing its total dividend for FY26 to 0.4 sen per share, or RM15.4 million.
Managing director Datuk S Y Gan said persistent global trade uncertainties and weak consumer demand had characterised much of the financial year.
He said customer orders had started to pick up ahead of the year-end festive season, with the group expecting the positive momentum to continue into the next quarter.
"Moreover, our customers are planning to roll out new models in the coming fiscal year to maintain market competitiveness.
"Over in the Philippines, the operations continued to make progress, with a higher utilisation rate as additional models entered production.
"While the plant has yet to reach the breakeven point required to cover fixed costs, utilisation has improved on the back of higher production output," he said.
31d6df844eacbe18: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 29 — Maritime Network Sdn Bhd is seeking a written explanation from the Royal Malaysian Customs Department (JKDM) following a meeting with the Ministry of Finance (MOF) over the handling of Atlanta crude discharged at Tanjung Langsat under a K8 declaration.
At the September 25 discussion, chaired by MOF Tax Division Under-Secretary Datuk John Patrick Antonysamy and attended by JKDM officers, the chair said no duty was due on the cargo as presented.
He also raised a separate question for Customs: how the K8 cargo was transferred to another party
Maritime Network said both points need to be recorded and explained in writing before the company can close its compliance file.
“If MOF’s position is that no duty is payable, we are asking for the provisions, exemptions and factual assumptions behind that conclusion. We will respect a reasoned answer.

“But a verbal conclusion cannot tell a shipping agent which documents supported a cargo transfer, what declaration closed the movement, or why the agent was compounded,” said Maritime Network managing director Datuk Seri R. Jeyenderan.

The meeting focused principally on approximately 42,051 tonnes associated with MT Invictus. Maritime has also separately raised questions about another Atlanta crude cargo carried by MT Marlin Santorini.
The two cargoes had a combined declared value of more than RM220 million. That figure represents their declared cargo value, not an estimate of unpaid tax.
Maritime Network said a K8 document discussed at the meeting was interpreted differently by those present.

Its representatives questioned whether an outward record continued to describe Atlanta crude despite reported blending into very low sulphur fuel oil, while an officer described the document shown as an inward movement between Customs stations.

Maritime Network is asking JKDM to resolve the issue using the full set of certified declarations, warehouse records and final movement documents. It is not asserting that a false outward declaration has been established.
The company is also requesting a separate review of a compound it says was imposed over manifest documentation.

It wants JKDM to state the precise alleged omission, why responsibility was assigned to Maritime, and what review route is available. MOF’s verbal conclusion on duty did not itself cancel the compound.
MIDA, in a written response dated September 17, said questions concerning activity at a Public Licensed Warehouse and applicable duties should be directed to JKDM.

Maritime Network said it is now seeking a coordinated written answer from MOF and Customs identifying the applicable legal instruments, any approvals or exemptions, and the records supporting their conclusions.
“This is not a request to declare somebody guilty. It is a request to show the governing rule and the transaction trail,” Jeyenderan said.

“If the process was permitted and no tax was due, put that reasoning on record. If a declaration needs correcting, say what should be corrected and by whom. Everyone in the industry needs an answer they can actually follow.”

Maritime Network said it would consider and fairly reflect any substantive written response from MOF or JKDM. It has not received an official written determination on the points discussed at the meeting as at the time of this draft.
b58050559c069c85: KUALA LUMPUR: Financial problems affecting UiTM Holdings Sdn Bhd, which resulted in millions of ringgit in losses, were not unknown to the university's management but had been discussed and monitored at the highest levels, a former university vice-chancellor said.

Professor Datuk Dr Roziah Mohd Janor said UiTM Holdings' management was required to regularly present financial reports to the company's board of directors before they were brought to the university management and Board of Directors.
"The management was aware of the matter, and the crisis faced by UiTM Holdings had been discussed at the university management level.

"They had also been audited by a special audit team as well as the National Audit Department. However, during my tenure as vice-chancellor, I requested that every investment and project under UiTM Holdings be presented," she said.

Roziah said the public needed to understand that UiTM Holdings was a holding company owned by the university and that its initial capital did not come from direct government contributions or allocations.
Instead, she said, the capital came from internal accumulated funds generated and collected by the university.
She said regulatory mechanisms had also been established at the university's highest level to monitor investment governance and risks.

"The governance of UiTM's Board of Directors, both during my tenure and now, is supported by UiTM Board of Directors committees, which have a specific role in monitoring the company's operations and investment risks.
"In my view, UiTM is now improving the situation, and follow-up action must be actively undertaken by the current management and board of directors to address the issue," she said.
Roziah said the issue of UiTM Holdings' losses should be viewed alongside efforts to rehabilitate the company and improve its governance to safeguard the university's interests.
She said recommendations for improvement made through the audit process and the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) should be given attention and implemented immediately.

In March 2024, PAC found that UiTM Holdings and its subsidiaries had yet to achieve their original objectives and mandate of creating wealth for UiTM, creating investment opportunities and strengthening the strategic position of the company's core businesses.

The PAC also found that capital injections totalling RM259.98 million by UiTM between 2007 and 2018 for its shareholding in UiTM Holdings were not in accordance with the Universiti Teknologi MARA Act 1976 as they had not obtained the approval of the Finance Minister.
The committee, among other recommendations, called on UiTM to tighten oversight of UiTM Holdings and ensure compliance in matters involving investments, loans and the establishment of subsidiaries.
The issue came under renewed scrutiny after Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last Saturday called for UiTM Holdings' management and governance to be reviewed.
He had said that weaknesses needed to be rectified, while firm action should be taken if any wrongdoing was found.

The Higher Education Ministry also said the process of reviewing and restructuring the holding companies of public universities, including UiTM Holdings, had begun last year to ensure the entities functioned more effectively and contributed to their respective universities.
UiTM Holdings was previously reported to have recorded cumulative pre-tax losses of about RM157 million for the 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021 financial years.

The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission also confirmed that an investigation launched in 2023 was still ongoing, including into issues related to the 50-megawatt solar project in Gambang, Pahang, and governance weaknesses that had been raised.

d331bfd982953672: After an unusual pitch to investors, Anthropic has laid bare its challenges in becoming anything like a profitable, normal business in its IPO prospectus. Posing an “existential risk to humanity” was among the messages reportedly intended to allure investors, as if to say, “We could make you rich, but also you might not live spend it.” The Reg has long suspected the apocalyptic schtick which has become de rigueur among AI model builders is suspiciously self-serving. It focuses attention on the supposed power of their technologies while also encouraging regulation of the sector once their claimed-to-be-race-winning horses have bolted. Nonetheless, the Financial Times points out that a third of Anthropic's prospectus talks about AI models with the ability to manipulate, blackmail and exhibit other unpredictable behaviours. Happy days. But what about brass tacks? According to the leaked figures, the maker of the Claude model favored among AI-assisted coders said it plans to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming years. That’s more than a quarter of its hoped-for value of $2 trillion. The company spent $7.33 billion on compute and infrastructure last year. Also according to the leaked doc, Anthropic made an operating loss of more than $8 billion last year, although revenue increased 12x to around $4.6 billion. While Anthropic courts investors with the end-of-the-world spiel, other news suggests we should question whether the underpinning of the AI economy is indeed sound. Oracle has promised to build $300 billion in datacenter capacity for OpenAI, a rival to Anthropic. However, it has issued a "force majeure" notice to Blue Owl, an alternative asset management company and specialist in private capital, according to reports. A force majeure is designed to allow signatories to opt out of contractual obligations in circumstances beyond their control. The concern lies around Oracle’s ability to get power to a large New Mexico datacenter, which Oracle says is going ahead as planned. Readers not drawn to the AI doomster narrative might pay heed to the other potential downside in the AI buildout, which is set to see $31.6 trillion in capital expenditure spent before 2050 to meet our supposed need for AI services. Current investment equates to around a third of all US economic growth, according to figures from August. Estimates earlier in the year put it higher. Were that to collapse, as the dotcom boom did, the effects on the world economy would be dire. With AI, discounting the worst that could happen does not offer much consolation. ®

Xu Song, 40, recently announced that he and Feng Xi, who is 14 years his junior, tied the knot after four years of dating.

The couple announced their marriage in a joint Weibo post, writing: "Our life story has entered a new chapter. Thank you for all your concern and well wishes."
They accompanied the announcement with two romantic wedding photos taken in a scenic grassland setting.
In one shot, Feng Xi wears a striking red wedding gown alongside Xu Song in a sleek black suit.
In another, she dons a classic white dress as the newlyweds hold hands and smile for the camera.
The pair initially kept their romance under wraps.
But shortly after Feng Xi finished filming a television programme, the two were spotted holding hands while out shopping before heading back home together.
They later made a rare public appearance at a New Year's Eve gala at the end of 2023.
When playful fans urged them to get married during the event, Xu Song quipped: "I can consider it!"
As it turns out he wasn't joking after all.

"The current relatively low Overnight Policy Rate has created a favourable environment for housebuyers and investors hence making homeownership more affordable.

Crescendo will monitor closely the market situation and implement appropriate measures, where necessary, to mitigate potential impacts on its operations.
"The group will adopt a prudent approach by leveraging on its strategic landbank to develop properties that meet market needs and manage the rising cost," it said.

7cd7200b881f6e07: SEPTEMBER 29 — The Negeri Sembilan’s Customary Land Tenure for Luak Tanah Mengandung Customary Land and Lingkungan Customary Land Enactment 2022 (En 20 of 2022) came into force on December 29, 2022.

It is an Enactment to amend the laws relating to customary land tenure for luak tanah mengandung customary land and lingkungan customary land and to provide for matters connected therewith and incidental thereto.
An Enactment is a State law.
The Preamble to the Enactment states as follows:

“WHEREAS luak tanah mengandung customary land and lingkungan customary land is an asset for the Malay community in Negeri Sembilan which has been administered in accordance with custom immemorial. When the Torrens system was introduced in Negeri Sembilan by the British before Independence, luak tanah mengandung customary land and lingkungan customary land tenure was codified as written laws (Customary Tenure Enactment [F.M.S. CAP. 215] and Customary Tenure (Lengkongan Lands) Enactment 1960 [Enactment 12] (Revised-2017)) to preserve the ownership of the said customary land and to protect the interests for the future generation of Perpatih Custom and Temenggung Custom communities in Negeri Sembilan which are also assured by Article 90 of the Federal Constitution;
“AND WHEREAS it is now that the said written laws need to be updated with respect of their implementation and legislation to be parallel with current development in land matters;
“AND WHEREAS State Legislative Assembly opines that the said written laws need to be updated;

“AND WHEREAS it is now expedient to make a law relating to luak tanah mengandung customary land and lingkungan customary land tenure for the purpose of amending and updating the laws of the said customary land tenure and to provide for matters connected therewith and incidental thereto.”

The Preamble concludes with the statement that the Enactment is enacted by the Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Ruling Chiefs of Negeri Sembilan with the advice and approval of the State Legislative Assembly.

At the second reading of the Bill, then Menteri Besar (MB) Datuk Seri Aminuddin Harun informed the Dewan Undangan Negeri (DUN) that there was a need to update the written laws governing Luak Tanah Mengandung and Lingkungan customary lands to ensure that the administration of these lands was more organized and systematic.
The Bill sought to achieve five objectives:
Amending the Customary Tenure (Lengkongan Lands) Enactment 1960;
Providing an authoritative text in the Malay language;
Updating the laws regarding Luak Tanah Mengandung and Lingkungan customary lands to align with current developments in land affairs;
Establishing new provisions concerning the development of Luak Tanah Mengandung and Lingkungan customary lands while upholding customary principles; and
Improving existing provisions to make them easier to understand and implement.

The MB further explained that the law would bring greater benefits to the State, as the new provisions would enable the development of luak tanah mengandung and lingkungan customary lands in the Kuala Pilah and Jempol districts without the need to revoke their customary land status, while simultaneously resolving the long-standing issue of neglected and abandoned customary lands plaguing the State.

Debates on the Bill then ensued. The ADUN for Rantau, Datuk Seri Utama Mohamad Hasan was first to stand up. Calling for caution as the Bill sought to amend customary land tenure, he wondered whether the Bill was constitutional and said (verbatim):

“[S]eingat sayalah Dato’ Yang Dipertua ya, apa saja berkenaan dengan adat, tak kira tanah atau apa ke, dia mesti diputuskan oleh Dewan Keadilan. Kerajaan Negeri tak boleh menceroboh kerana kita adanya Undang-Undang Tubuh.

“Adat dijagakan oleh … Dewan Keadilan [dan Undang]. Kita tak boleh campur melainkan kalau Dewan Keadilan memutuskan, yang mana keputusan Dewan Keadilan ini tidak boleh dicabar di mana-mana mahkamah. Dia merupakan keputusan tertinggi. Saya nak tahu, nak tanyalah ya, sama ada Dewan Keadilan telah pun memerintahkannya.

“Kalau tidak Dato’ Dipertua … kita membuat sesuatu yang unconstitutional. Kalau dah ada, okaylah. Tapi saya tak nampak ada dalam preamble dia mengatakan bahawa Kerajaan Negeri telah pun mendapat arahan daripada Dewan Keadilan yang bermesyuarat sekian-sekian tarikh, sekian-sekian minit.”
Similar concerns were expressed by ADUN Linggi, Datuk Abdul Rahman Mohd Redza who stood next to debate.
Linggi said (verbatim):

“Kalau kita nak ubah undang-undang lama Dato’ Yang Dipertua, perlu datang daripada Dewan Keadilan kerana kuasa di bawah Dewan Keadilan ini adalah muktamad dan mengatasi kuasa executive dan mengatasi kuasa legislature.

“Untuk menjelaskan status ataupun kedudukan adat di Negeri Sembilan ini, kita lihat bahawa wujudnya pengasingan kuasa ataupun separation of powers antara bidang kuasa adat dan bidang kuasa sivil dalam Undang-Undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan.

“Kalau kita lihat Artikel 40 Undang-Undang Tubuh, Raja hendaklah bertindak atas nasihat. Duli Yang Maha Mulia Tuanku hendaklah menjalan kewajipannya atas nasihat exco…. [U]ntuk perkara-perkara lain, Tuanku dikehendaki untuk menjalankan tanggungjawabnya mengikut nasihat exco kecuali … berkaitan adat Melayu. Jadi bila berkaitan dengan adat Melayu, Duli Yang Maha Mulia Tuanku tak perlu dengar nasihat exco sebaliknya dia perlu menerima nasihat Dewan Keadilan kerana bidang kuasa adat adalah bidang kuasa Dewan Keadilan.”

As regards the concerns raised by Rantau, it turned out that meetings of the Dewan Keadilan were held on March 3, 2022 and June 17, 2022 as the DUN was informed of minutes of the meetings by the MB before the Bill was put to vote.
The Bill was subsequently passed at the second and third readings by a vote of 19 “Ayes” and 16 abstentions.
Despite the grave concerns raised by the opposition, all 16 opposition ADUNs abstained instead of voting “Noes”.
As Linggi had said in the DUN, the jurisdiction over Malay custom falls within the purview of the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang.

Now, if the Ruler does not need to act on the advice of the executive on matters of adat but must act on the advice of the Dewan Keadilan, why was the advice of the same not acted on, leading to the crisis in the State?
The Dewan Keadilan has reaffirmed that Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir remains the legitimate Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negri Sembilan.
Rantau had asserted in the DUN, the Dewan Keadilan is the highest authority on adat in the State.

d8851f53c3590797: LONDON: Mauricio Pochettino has branded Manchester City's era of sustained success "a period of deception" after they were reportedly found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.
City are believed to have been found guilty of breaching the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them.
News of the decision, reached by an independent commission, was widely reported on Friday but no official announcement has been made by the Premier League.
City have strenuously denied the charges and their chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak on Saturday said he is still confident of proving the club's innocence.
City have won a host of trophies, including the Premier League and Champions League, since the takeover by their Abu Dhabi-based owners in 2008.
US manager Pochettino spent seven years in the Premier League as Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton boss.
The Argentine believes City's guilt has done massive damage to both the club and the Premier League as a whole.
"Whatever punishment, it's impossible to turn back time," Pochettino told reporters.
"It's done a lot of damage. Many clubs followed the rules and some didn't.

"It is a huge sadness. We get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn't that real, what seemed good maybe wasn't so good, what didn't look good maybe was good but couldn't be good because of what happened.

"We went through something where sporting fairness didn't exist. So, how do you repair everything that was damaged because of that, if it's true all of the 114 rules that were broken, we've lived through a period of deception," he said.
The charges relate to a period from 2009-2010 to 2017-2018, with City also accused of failing to co-operate with Premier League investigations between December 2018 and February 2023.
City are expected to appeal against their eventual punishment, which is yet to be announced and could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine.
There have also been calls for City to be stripped of the Premier League titles won since 2008.

Pochettino recently said Chelsea should be stripped of the 2016-2017 Premier League title after being found guilty of historical rule breaches, adding that the trophy should be given to his Tottenham side, who finished runners-up that season.
However, Pochettino is unsure of a fitting sanction for City.
"What are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points? It's really hard," he said.
"If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham - I remember building the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months.

"Tottenham was fighting for titles with those above us and every year in the top four, getting to the semi-finals of the Champions League without being able to do a transfer for 18 months, all because we needed to get used to the Premier League financial controls?
"They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that's why I say: it's all very strange," he said.

9267178dd42da12b: KUALA LUMPUR: As Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad bade his final farewell to his late wife, Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, yesterday, three medical personnel stayed close by, watching over the former prime minister.

What caught the public's attention was not just their presence, but the sight of the three — a Malay doctor, an Indian nurse and a Chinese therapist — standing together as they accompanied the 101-year-old former prime minister through one of the most difficult moments of his life.
One of the three was Dr Iskandar Mirza Amran, a Clinical Cardiology Fellow and Specialist in Internal Medicine at the National Heart Institute (IJN).
Dr Iskandar, 40, said he was tasked with caring for Dr Mahathir throughout the funeral.

He said there were seven people in IJN's team of seven who treated and supervised Dr Mahathir and his late wife. The team is headed by Datuk Dr Amin Ariff Nuruddin and Datuk Dr Ahmad Khairuddin Mohamed Yusof; and also included Datuk Dr Ghazali Ahmad; Dr Hafidz Abd Hadi; Dr Hisham Md Sharom; Dr Afif Ashaari; and himself.
"Last Sunday, I was on a 24-hour shift. Yesterday morning, we received a 'code blue', which meant an emergency involving Dr Hasmah.
"I was among those called on to perform CPR on her before her passing was confirmed," he said when contacted.
Dr Iskandar said he was then tasked with accompanying Dr Mahathir throughout the burial, as other doctors in the team were attending to another important procedure.
"I saw that Dr Mahathir was grieving. He did not say much, and only wept.
"I checked on him to see if he was experiencing breathing difficulties or chest pains, but he told me he did not have any of those symptoms," he said.
On the viral image of him with two other medical personnel - an Indian nurse and a Chinese therapist - Dr Iskandar said he did not think that the image would touch so many Malaysians.
"I can't deny that the public perception of doctors has deteriorated of late due to various factors. That image changed the people's perception.
"Many people contacted me to thank me for taking care of Tun Mahathir. I'm pleased that our presence managed to affect the negative perception towards doctors.
"When I hear the thanks and appreciation from the people, it makes the exhaustion from working for 40 hours worthwhile," he said.
Dr Hasmah, who was 100-years-old, died at the IJN at 9.20am yesterday.
She was buried at the National Cemetery, Presint 20, Putrajaya.
a3594f42920255ca: Investors appear to be betting that AI will deliver substantial gains in software engineering productivity, according to economists who used stock market movements to estimate the technology's expected impact. Economists affiliated with the University of California, Berkeley (UCB) and the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) say that between November 2022 and December 2025, "AI increased the market's expected present value of software engineering productivity by the equivalent of a permanent 32.6 percent productivity increase." Alex Blumenfeld (UCB), Jonathon Hazell (LSE), Chen Lian (UCB), and Andreas Schaab (UCB) describe their findings in a National Bureau of Economics Research paper titled "The Macroeconomic Effect of AI: Sizing the Software Engineering Channel." The authors argue that investors have increasingly priced anticipated gains from AI development tools into company valuations since the introduction of ChatGPT in November 2022. "We empirically measure whether firms with larger software engineering payroll shares experience larger stock-price increases when the AI stock index rises," explained Chen Lian, assistant professor of finance at UC Berkeley, in an email to The Register. "We then use an economic model to translate that relationship into the AI-driven software engineering productivity gains investors anticipate. "A preliminary look at our data suggests that total software engineering employment among the firms covered has increased over the past few years. But our productivity estimate does not depend on that employment trend at all." Rather than measuring developers' output directly, the researchers examined how company stock returns respond to news about AI and whether that response varies with the proportion of each company's payroll devoted to software engineering. "By 'news about AI,' we mean new information reflected in stock prices," explained Lian. "As discussed above, we combine empirical measurements with an economic model to infer how AI has changed investors' expectations of software engineering productivity and the implied GDP impact." Lian acknowledges that market expectations may not fully materialize. "Our estimates capture the market’s assessment of current and future productivity gains, and markets can be overly optimistic or pessimistic," he said. "The advantage is a forward-looking measure, available in real time, when many of AI's effects have yet to play out." The market-implied productivity gain of 32.6 percent is comparable in magnitude to the 21-56 percent acceleration on individual tasks reported by other researchers, the authors say. They note however that task-level gains can be offset by bottlenecks that limit productivity gains. In the context of software development that might take the form of code reviews that can't keep pace with surging commit figures. Feeding the estimated productivity gain into their economic model also produces a sizeable implied effect on GDP. "News about AI from November 2022 to December 2025 corresponds to a present-value GDP increase equivalent to a permanent 3.61 percent level increase," the authors report. As to whether the productivity gains seen in software engineering are extensible to other industry sectors, Lian said: "Our methods can be used to study the economic impact of AI through other channels, which we plan to explore in follow-up work." ®

843624b20d6b18e1: LOS ANGELES: Courteney Cox has revealed she spent eight years fighting to get her new true-crime movie, Evil Genius, off the ground.

Starring Patricia Arquette and David Harbour, the dark comedy thriller recently premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival.
Inspired by the notorious 2003 "pizza bomber" case in Erie, Pennsylvania, the film is another milestone in Cox's long career.

That determination proved essential for Evil Genius.

"It was really hard to get off the ground," Cox explained. "There was a lockdown and two different strikes. I've been working on it for eight years through all of that, and I just couldn't let it go. I had to make this. I fought and fought through all these obstacles."
The film tells the tragic story of pizza delivery driver Brian Wells, who died in 2003 when a bomb locked around his neck exploded following a bank robbery.
Cox became hooked on the case after watching the 2018 Netflix documentary series Evil Genius. She wanted to understand the minds behind such a strange and complex crime.

9f0c40a600177d43: SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time yesterday and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, although engine trouble cut short a planned six-orbit flight. Super Heavy had problems of its own. All 33 Raptor 3 engines ignited at 07:48 CT, but one shut down during ascent. The booster later reignited 26 of the 28 engines planned for its boostback maneuver. During descent, it reignited 11 of the planned 13 engines for the high-thrust portion of its landing burn before stepping down to five and then three. It splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, after which its flight termination system was deliberately triggered to test the safety hardware. More consequential was the premature shutdown of one of Starship's three vacuum-optimized Raptors during ascent. The remaining five engines burned longer to compensate, leaving the spacecraft on its planned suborbital trajectory. This ensured it would return to Earth even if controllers lost control, but also meant a further burn was required to enter orbit. Controllers then had to decide whether enough propulsion redundancy remained to perform both the orbital insertion maneuver and, crucially, the later deorbit burn. According to SpaceX, all three sea-level Raptors remained healthy, so controllers gave the go-ahead to relight one and complete the climb to orbit. After deploying the satellites, Starship began its coast around Earth, but controllers cut short most of the intended ten-hour flight "out of an abundance of caution." It performed its deorbit burn and splashed down in the North Pacific after about three hours. Unlike the Flight 13 vehicle, which survived its landing and was recovered, this one toppled over and exploded shortly after hitting the water. Reaching orbit, deploying an operational payload, and executing a controlled deorbit represent major advances for Starship. However the premature Raptor shutdown remains a concern given the launch cadence required for a lunar landing. NASA's inspector general said SpaceX's lunar architecture calls for a propellant depot followed by more than ten tanker launches, potentially at intervals of about six days. SpaceX has yet to demonstrate vehicle-to-vehicle propellant transfer in orbit. That tanker campaign is not required for the revised Artemis III mission in 2027, which is now a docking demonstration in low Earth orbit rather than a lunar landing. SpaceX's contribution will be a single Version 3 Starship fitted with a docking system so that Orion can rendezvous with it; astronauts will remain aboard Orion. Orbital refueling and the rapid succession of tanker launches will become critical for the first crewed landing, which NASA now assigns to Artemis IV in 2028. ®

b75c7cc06e76e96a: TEHRAN, Sept 29 — Iran today threatened to attack infrastructure around the Middle East, intensifying its rhetoric as it awaits a formal response from Washington on a new plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump has already dismissed the proposal from Tehran, but Iran’s foreign minister said yesterday that he was expecting a formal response from American officials in the coming day.
Fighting has subsided in recent weeks, though Tehran has continued to target ships in the strait, with Washington falling back on an economic pressure campaign instead of further military action.
Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf today threatened new attacks, saying no infrastructure in the region would be safe if his country’s security was not guaranteed.

“In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either; or if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will remain safe,” Ghalibaf, who is also Iran’s parliament speaker, said according to video released by state TV.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he expected a formal answer from the US today to Tehran’s proposal, state media reported.
Iran has maintained a blockade on commercial shipping through Hormuz since the war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic.
The shipping route carried a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the conflict began.
The US military has been maintaining a counterblockade of Iran’s ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting oil.
Conditions

Araghchi said late yesterday that Qatari intermediaries “presented ideas, and we discussed them; they are set to raise the matter with the American side once more, after which the final US response will be conveyed to us”.
The top diplomat, who was in New York for the UN General Assembly, said “the Qataris hope this will be done by tomorrow”.
“The current focus is solely on the Strait of Hormuz, and the reopening of the strait is contingent upon the fulfilment of certain conditions that we have communicated to the other side,” he added.
Last week, discussions were held in New York between Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
As a precondition for ending its blockade, Iran is demanding a seven-day ceasefire across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah is regularly bombarded by Israel.
It is also demanding the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade on its ports.
Both sides claim to have control of Hormuz, with the US saying oil is moving through and Tehran insisting the waterway is closed.
Today, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of the country’s military, said “the US claim that it remains open is false”.

“Sneaking a few hundred barrels of oil through under the cover of darkness — with transponders turned off and at great cost — does not constitute the strait being open,” said spokesperson Hossein Mohebi.
“A truly open strait is one where, as in the past, at least 125 vessels would pass through daily, transporting a minimum of 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum products.
“Any vessel attempting to pass through sustains damage — either we strike it, or it hits a mine,” he added. — AFP

4b45088e56e2beaa: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 29 — The Madani Government will not allow the problem of foreign refugee presence to persist indefinitely; instead, it has begun resolving the issue firmly, systematically, and in stages based on the Constitution and the rule of law, said Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail.

“This implementation is coordinated by the Ministry of Home Affairs together with the Malaysian Immigration Department and related agencies. This resolution was also achieved through diplomatic approaches and direct negotiations with the Myanmar Government,” he said in a statement today.

Saifuddin Nasution noted that the presence of foreign refugees, particularly from Myanmar, has dragged on for decades without a definitive resolution, turning into a massive financial burden for the country, triggering serious social crises, and posing a tangible security threat to the citizens.

He said that for issues involving two countries, enforcement actions alone are insufficient; instead, they require cooperation from the country of origin to enable the acceptance, documentation, and repatriation processes to be carried out in an orderly and phased manner.
“This is the approach we are taking: the law is upheld, enforcement is implemented, and diplomatic channels are utilised to produce a solution.

“Although Malaysia is not a State Party to the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol, we choose a firm yet civilised approach centered on the values of compassion and the spirit of ASEAN familyhood, with every action executed in an orderly and responsible manner without compromising national security and sovereignty,” he said.

Saifuddin Nasution stated that today’s first phase was just a beginning, while subsequent phases will proceed as soon as the identification, documentation, verification, and operational readiness processes are completed.

“We are beginning to resolve a legacy problem that has dragged on for a long time, based on the law. We safeguard national sovereignty. The security, welfare, and interests of Malaysian citizens remain the top priority.”
A total of 1,476 Myanmar refugee detainees - comprising 1,370 men, 79 women, and 27 children - were repatriated at the Royal Malaysian Navy (RMN) Base in Lumut, Perak, today.
The repatriation process was carried out using Myanmar Navy ships, namely the UMS Moattama, escort vessel UMS King Sin Phyu Shin, and medical ship UMS Thanlwin. — Bernama

Both sides claim to have control of Hormuz, with the US saying oil is moving through and Tehran insisting the waterway is closed.
On Tuesday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of the country's military, said "the US claim that it remains open is false".

"Sneaking a few hundred barrels of oil through under the cover of darkness - with transponders turned off and at great cost - does not constitute the strait being open," said spokesman Hossein Mohebi.
"A truly open strait is one where, as in the past, at least 125 vessels would pass through daily, transporting a minimum of 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum products.

ccace86cfc2f2989: The Reform leader’s reaction to the RAF Fairford affair is again revealing. If what’s needed is a steady hand and cool head, he’s not the guy Another week, another chance for Nigel Farage to demonstrate his literally hysterical leadership inabilities. For a guy who supposedly valorises the wartime British spirit, Nigel would genuinely have had to have been interned during that conflict on account of his serial predilection for spreading panic and unverified information at any given chance. b05f29b1e415e34c: KUALA LUMPUR: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has agreed to designate Sept 29 as Malaysian Professionals Day.
"When it was proposed that Sept 29 be Malaysian Professionals Day, I agreed because it makes sense and serves a purpose," he said.
Anwar was speaking at the inaugural Professionals Conference & Exhibition (Profex 2026) at the KLGCC Convention Centre here today.
He said the professional class was central to national progress, adding that political leaders, civil servants and professionals had to work as one team.

Citing Spanish thinker José Ortega y Gasset, Anwar cautioned that specialisation must not come at the expense of a wider understanding of society, referring to what the thinker called the "barbarism of specialisation".
"Building a city is not only about buildings and concrete.
"If we build only from narrow, specialised viewpoints, we will build a concrete jungle," he said.

Anwar said the pursuit of excellence was also embedded in cultures and faiths familiar to Malaysians, citing the concepts of wasatiyyah (moderation) in Islam, Zhongyong (Doctrine of the Mean) in Confucianism and the "Golden Mean" in the Greek tradition.
The prime minister also warned that professionals could not escape responsibility for governance failures.
"When we look at past scandals, whether 1MDB, Tabung Haji or Felda, the political leadership is responsible, of course. But the professional class is not spared either," he said.
He said many people knew about wrongdoing but remained silent.
"Most people know but cannot speak out. Top professionals know their own field but are deaf and mute about everything else," he said.
Anwar said no country could survive if corruption was tolerated.

Meanwhile, he said he would bring proposals on engaging professionals to the Cabinet and asked Balai Ikhtisas Malaysia's leadership to identify experts in areas such as health, education and information technology.
"Remember, ministers, we do not have expertise in every area. We should listen and evaluate," he said.

f73ffd0bcaba2a72: SEREMBAN: Police have arrested another 16-year-old male student to assist in the investigation into the death of a Form Two student in Kuala Pilah last Friday.

10831acfbe24029d: Two former leaders of IBM's X-Force Red team have launched RemoteThreat, an offensive cybersecurity startup backed by $7 million in pre-seed funding. CEO Chris Thompson and CTO Shawn Jones say the company's platform uses AI to plan, execute, and adapt offensive cyber operations, extending beyond the continuous penetration testing and vulnerability detection offered by other automated security tools. Thompson and Jones previously ran X-Force Red, where their team was hired to test nuclear power plants, critical infrastructure, and major banks. In May 2024, Thompson told The Register how X-Force used AI to break into a semiconductor manufacturer's network in eight hours. The pair subsequently created Offensive AI Con, an invitation-only research event whose second edition is scheduled for early October. "We're looking at how noisy but very capable frontier models are right now, and we started to think: What happens when they can do what we can do as one of the best groups of red-teamers in the world?" Thompson told The Register in an interview. He said the concern was that AI could produce custom malware approaching the quality used by state-sponsored attackers, then deploy it at unprecedented speed and scale. RemoteThreat's 15 employees include senior operators, security researchers, engineers, and malware developers from X-Force Adversary Services, Mandiant, SpecterOps, Dreadnode, Bugcrowd, Microsoft, defense contractors, and government agencies. RemoteThreat says its platform gives defenders and government operators access to the same speed and scale that AI may offer their adversaries. According to the startup, its customers already include a major bank, a securities exchange operator, a large US healthcare company, and a leading AI lab. "We're focused on preparing these Fortune 500 organizations to better simulate this nation-state level of attack," Thompson said. "And then on the flip side, provide the government with the tooling to target their adversaries as quickly as possible." RemoteThreat describes its platform as eight connected systems covering mission planning, command and control, implants, initial access, advanced attack capabilities, obfuscation, analysis, and AI-assisted operations. Given the obvious potential for misuse, RemoteThreat says access is restricted to vetted enterprises, defense contractors, and US government customers. The platform uses small, purpose-built models for some tasks. Customers can also connect models from OpenAI or Anthropic, or use an open-weight alternative, giving the chosen LLM access to what Thompson described as "1,000 tools that we've built from scratch." The platform can be operated by either humans or AI agents. Customers can "drive a lot of this testing from your Codex terminal instead of having to log into our website, for example," Thompson said. RemoteThreat says its capabilities can run within the complete platform or be integrated as components of partners' products. It has teamed up with Talon Defense, which supplies AI and cyber technology to national security, defense, and intelligence customers. RemoteThreat has also partnered with the Nakasone Group, the national security advisory firm founded by retired US Army Gen. Paul Nakasone, former director of the National Security Agency and commander of US Cyber Command. Nakasone is also a strategic adviser to the startup. The launch comes as Washington seeks a larger private-sector role in offensive cyber operations. The US Cyber Strategy published in March calls for closer cooperation with industry on defensive and offensive missions. An August presidential memorandum goes further, ordering the creation of a program through which vetted US companies may conduct cyber operations against foreign cybercrime groups under federal direction and oversight. RemoteThreat also says it has joined US Special Operations Command's Special Operations Forces Rapid Acquisition Consortium for Emerging Requirements, or SOF RACER, which provides a route for supplying capabilities to special operations forces. Thompson expects the government to make greater use of commercially developed offensive cyber products, both to support existing mission teams and to pursue cybercriminal groups. "It's a bit of a gold rush in this space because this is the first time, across every major program, the government is being pushed to work with the commercial sector," he said. RemoteThreat is positioning itself to supply the picks and shovels – albeit ones capable of breaking into somebody else's network. ®

88cad12fedcb1836: KUALA LUMPUR: Gamuda Bhd anticipates its earnings performance next year will be predominantly anchored by domestic construction projects, including hyperscale data centre builds, following strong domestic segment performance this year.

Its net profit rose 5.2 per cent in Q4 FY26 to RM349.7 million, driven mainly by stronger contributions from its domestic construction projects, while revenue jumped 19 per cent year-on-year to RM5.76 billion.
For the full financial year, net profit rose five per cent to RM1.05 billion from RM1 billion, while revenue increased 14 per cent to a record RM18.6 billion from RM15.97 billion.

"The group broke its earnings record for the fifth consecutive year…driven by robust contributions from domestic construction projects and high margin quick-turnaround projects (QTP) in Vietnam," said Gamuda in the filing with Bursa Malaysia.

The group said its property division recorded a 14 per cent decline in quarterly revenue and a 41 per cent drop in net profit, mainly due to slower sales conversion across its townships in Malaysia.

Net gearing stood at 72 per cent at end-July 2026, temporarily exceeding the group's self-imposed 70 per cent limit following land acquisitions in Vietnam and Singapore earlier this year to replenish its portfolio of quick-turnaround projects.
"The group's continued ability to generate operating cashflow to fund its capex is evidenced by the near RM800 million surplus cash generated from its operating activities during the year," it said.
Gamuda expects its gearing to decline from next year, supported by cash inflows from its record construction orderbook and RM7.6 billion in unbilled property sales.

30a167d46a238f7b: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 29 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the Malaysian government will continue engaging with Myanmar to find an amicable solution to the long-standing issue of refugees.
He said the issue, which has remained unresolved for decades, had become more complicated as the number of refugees increased, including through negotiations on their possible return.
“That is why in our negotiations, we tie all these together.
“It is easy for them to say: ‘Don’t send them back.’ Where are we going to put these hundreds of thousands?

“So now what we want are conditions so that there is safety. That is why we invited them to negotiate,” he told reporters when met after launching the Professional Conference and Exhibition 2026 (PROFEX 2026) in conjunction with the Malaysia Professional Day.
He said without resolve and negotiations, it may lead to protests.
Anwar, in expressing appreciation that the Myanmar President had accepted the invitation, has said to allow the matter to be discussed and negotiated.

“So I’m glad that the President is kind enough to accept the invitation and we use that opportunity to discuss, negotiate and even when they agreed to bring back some of these refugees, of course we have to make sure they’ll be protected and whatever facilities be accorded.
“But just to say don’t send them back… There are a lot of concerns here too.
“No country can just accept hundreds of thousands and some countries millions. You have to be able to negotiate,” he added.
He said that the Malaysian government’s position is to protect the refugees’ welfare, human rights concerns.
“But to just condemn us for taking this initiative, I don’t think it’s fair.
“We are trying to find an amicable resolution to this issue.
“That is why I’ve invited him to continue to negotiate and see the parameters… how to resolve this.”
Further commenting, Anwar said, so far the ones sent, they will bring back their people.
“What else can we do? At least we take the trouble.
“Just push them back? No, it’s not true to say just push them back.
“We will first negotiate,” he said.
Anwar said the decision to invite the Myanmar President was important.
“They’ve been there. It’s not a perfect system.
“Some people say that ours is not perfect system too. Many countries are not perfect but still being recognised.”
“I’ve always said there’s the hypocrisy, as many of the countries in the West have been shouting against us but they can accept the atrocities by the Israeli government.
“And when it comes to here, we are trying to resolve,” he said.

2478aac7a24bd35e: PETALING JAYA: S&P Global Ratings has affirmed Malaysia’s sovereign credit ratings on the back of its robust economic growth, improving fiscal performance and monetary policy flexibility.
While the rating agency gave a positive assessment of the country’s economy, it also warned the ratings may be lowered over the next 24 months if political stability in Malaysia deteriorates.

In affirming its A– long-term and A-2 short-term foreign currency sovereign credit ratings as well as its A long-term and A-1 short-term local currency ratings, S&P also said the outlook on its long-term ratings is "stable".

It said Malaysia’s “consistently strong economic growth” and high degree of monetary policy flexibility underpin the sovereign ratings. In addition, its external position is supported by moderate current account surpluses and a large export base.
Malaysia’s external position has “historically been a ratings strength”, with the country having consistent current account surpluses for more than two decades, it added.

“The stable rating outlook reflects our expectation that Malaysia's growth momentum and prevailing policy environment will allow steady fiscal performance over the next two to three years,” S&P said in a statement.

It said Malaysia’s strong growth was led by the AI-driven investment cycle and high energy prices against a backdrop of relative political stability – an important factor in the government’s ability to achieve further fiscal and debt consolidation.
Net general government debt as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) decreased marginally to 69.5% in 2025, and S&P expects it to fall further to 67.8% this year.
It noted that the Pakatan Harapan-led coalition appears to have achieved a degree of political stability following a period of frequent changes in government between 2018 and 2022.

“While the relative stability of the Anwar Ibrahim administration has resulted in a more predictable policymaking environment, policy uncertainties may grow as the prospects of general elections increase.
“Political stability will be imperative to achieve further economic reforms and fiscal consolidation,” it said.
S&P also noted that Malaysia’s institutions have supported generally effective policymaking. “We believe the depth of institutional strength mitigates the risk of political instability,” it added.
The rating agency also flagged rising private-sector external borrowings as a potential pressure point for Malaysia’s external position.

The country’s total external debt stood at RM1.51 trillion, or 70.1% of GDP, at end-June 2026. It attributed part of the increase to corporate borrowing to finance specialised IT and data centre equipment amid the digital investment upcycle.
S&P also said it could raise Malaysia’s ratings over the next two to three years if its external position improves materially or fiscal outcomes outperform its forecasts.

Other international rating agencies have also reaffirmed Malaysia’s sovereign credit ratings. Moody’s affirmed Malaysia at A3 in July while Fitch maintained it at BBB+ in its December 2025 review, both with a stable outlook.
This means that Malaysia holds investment-grade sovereign credit ratings from all three major global rating agencies.

01e5b4ff59905364: PETALING JAYA: Persatuan Majikan Perindustrian, Komersial dan Perkhidmatan Malaysia (Micsea) menggesa kerajaan agar menilai dan melaksanakan dengan teliti kadar gaji minimum baharu secara berperingkat dalam Belanjawan 2027.

99603b66fdab106e: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 29 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today called on Malaysia’s professional community to move beyond narrow specialisation and work across disciplines.

“Professionals needed to integrate their specialised knowledge with a broader understanding of society, culture and the country’s needs, rather than working in isolation.

“What is great about professional life is that it brings together people from different disciplines, different races and different regions,” he said when launching the Professional Conference and Exhibition 2026 (PROFEX 2026) in conjunction with the Malaysia Professional Day.
Anwar added that professionals should not view one another through the lens of race, religion or region, but instead build stronger common ground around what was right, just and fair.
He said this was particularly important as Malaysia navigated rapid technological and economic changes, with new areas of expertise emerging in fields such as computing and digital transformation.
The Prime Minister stressed that specialisation should be accompanied by integration, including an understanding of one’s responsibilities towards family, society and the wider world.
He also urged professionals not to remain silent when confronted with dishonesty, corruption and abuses, saying professional responsibility extended beyond technical expertise.
“No country can ever survive in a system that allows cheating, corruption and excesses, and a lack of professionalism,” he said.
Anwar said professionals therefore have a responsibility to contribute towards strengthening governance and ensuring that systems served the country and its people.
“Malaysia’s future depended on professionals who could work together despite differences in culture and religion, while maintaining a strong commitment to justice and fairness.
“This is a national issue. It is relevant to all of us, and professionals in particular have a responsibility to ensure that this nation succeeds.

“And this nation succeeds through unity, through understanding gaps, respect — respect for our differences, cultural and religious — but more importantly, we need a strong sense of commitment to what is right, what is just and what is fair,” he said.

Anwar’s remarks come a day after he similarly called for technological advancement, including artificial intelligence and digital transformation, to remain grounded in ethics, culture and societal values.

Speaking at the International Future Conference 2026 in Kuala Lumpur yesterday, he said discussions about the future should not be confined to algorithms, computing power or economic outcomes, but should also incorporate philosophy, history and moral considerations.

PROFEX 2026, held under the theme “Uniting Professions, Transforming Malaysia’s Future”, brings together professionals, industry leaders, academia, government agencies and emerging talent, with an emphasis on interdisciplinary collaboration, knowledge exchange and professional development.
e10fd5ac1314c061: Campaigners against Palantir's involvement in the UK's health sector are set to make themselves heard this week with planned protests at the Labour Party conference and in London. The groups are among those urging the government not to extend the Palantir-led Federated Data Platform (FDP) contract, which could be worth up to £330 million over seven years. In June, the cross-party Science, Innovation and Technology Committee said Palantir should not play such a significant role in the UK public sector. Palantir won the lead role in the £330 million FDP contract in November 2023 following a procurement process that NHS England maintains was open and fair. The award followed £60 million in COVID-era NHS contracts awarded without competition. NHS England and Palantir say the platform links data held in disparate systems, helping hospitals use beds and operating theatres more efficiently and tackle the care backlog. The campaign groups protesting in Liverpool today say September 30 is the contractual deadline for Palantir to provide NHS England with an exit plan should the government choose not to continue the arrangement. The contract's initial term ends early next year, after which the government can extend it for two years, followed by two further one-year extensions. Questions are also being raised about the evidence used to support claims for the FDP's performance. Organizations opposing the rollout include the British Medical Association (BMA), public sector union UNISON, and the United Tech and Allied Workers Union. Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a No Palantir in the NHS campaigner at MedAct, said: "Patients and NHS staff are united in their opposition to this contract, and the last three years have seen unprecedented levels of professional and patient campaigning. Over 85,000 patients have made formal complaints to their hospitals. The government has an urgent opportunity to choose patients and staff over big tech, it must take it." Just Treatment spokesperson Hope Worsdale said: "Patients and health workers across England want Palantir out of our NHS. A company with a track record in surveillance, military technology and complicity in human rights abuses shouldn't be anywhere near our personal health data." Palantir says its software is helping UK public bodies carry out more NHS operations, keep Royal Navy ships at sea for longer and tackle domestic violence. It maintains that the data processed through the FDP belongs to the NHS and that disclosing it to anyone else would breach its contract. ®

dca90bdd5204984a: Earlier this month, the UN announced the planet will tip past 1.5 ˚C of warming, “likely within the next few years,” squashing any lingering hope that nations would cut emissions fast enough to achieve the loftiest goal of the Paris climate agreement.

In the US, the world’s second-largest-emitting country, its leader continues to deny climate realities and unravel climate policies. Big Tech is backpedaling on its climate ambitions, as companies race to build massive AI data centers.
And all this comes amid yet another season of shattered heat records, raging wildfires, and deadly floods.

It can be tempting to give in to climate doom and defeatism. But despite the headwinds, the world has still made incredible progress. Companies are developing and deploying renewables, batteries, and EVs; inventing cleaner means of producing industrial goods; and devising ways to keep cities and people safe even in the face of more extreme weather conditions.
Those advances will only accelerate as costs decline and people demand greater climate action, as well as all the economic and health benefits that come with it.
Recognizing our ability to make such progress is why MIT Technology Review began publishing our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch three years ago.

Once a year the editors and writers use their deep industry knowledge and academic sources to compile a long list of companies around the world that are transforming the way we generate energy, produce goods, move people and things, or mitigate rising climate dangers.

We then conduct several rounds of spirited newsroom debate to winnow that list down to 10 that we believe have done the most, or have the best chance, to make a real dent in emissions or improve public safety and health.

We’re happy to say we’ve finalized that list for 2026, and will publish it on October 6. You can sign up for The Download newsletter to be among the first to see it, or subscribe to receive full access to this year’s list. It features a mix of companies making strides in energy storage, nuclear power, transportation, and other areas, including ones that have figured out how to continue to make progress amid the regressive climate politics of the moment.

We hope you’ll enjoy the package and perhaps come away feeling a bit more hopeful that we can move fast enough to avoid the gravest dangers of climate change, and build a safer, healthier, and more sustainable world.
